https://www.politico.eu/article/france-c.text: LONDON — France and Canada will join the U.K. in imposing new trade sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in a major diplomatic boost for Britain as it toughens its stance on Israel. In the House of Commons Tuesday, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband confirmed Britain, France and Canada will impose a ban on the trade of goods and some services from Israeli settlements, having last month condemned Israel’s plans for 1,200 new homes in the E1 area east of Jerusalem. In response, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said the British consulate in Jerusalem will be closed, and warned “countermeasures” could be taken against other countries acting “against Israel.” Advertisement Advertisement The U.K., France and Canada are among 11 countries which issued a joint statement Tuesday warning the Israeli government’s actions in the West Bank are threatening the two-state solution. Miliband told MPs the British government “agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank,” adding that “all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this.” He said the U.K. will take action against specific companies and individuals who provide services such as construction, infrastructure, financing, or real estate for settlement expansion. Britain will “act in concert with others in a broad international coalition,” he said, adding that France and Canada will also ban the import of goods from illegal settlements. Confirming France’s involvement in a post on X , the country’s foreign affairs minister Jean-Noël Barrot said: “France cannot, through its trade, support a situation that threatens the security of both Israelis and Palestinians.” Anita Anand, the Canadian foreign affairs minister, said her country will introduce restrictions “in the coming months.” Advertisement Advertisement The coordinated announcement follows a major diplomatic effort by the British government over the summer, which culminated in a visit to Downing Street by French President Emmanuel Macron last week. Change of tone Miliband’s announcement marks a sharp shift in Britain’s stance on Israeli settlements under new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. The foreign secretary told MPs Britain “should have acted earlier,” and it had taken a change of prime minister “to come in and recognize the gravity of the situation.” In a press statement to camera, Sa’ar accused Miliband of telling “outrageous lies” in the British parliament and acting for “domestic political reasons” ahead of the ruling Labour Party’s annual conference this month. Israel also said will deny 12 MPs and British nationals entry to Israel, including veteran Labour MP Diane Abbott and the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, who has since been expelled from the party. The relationship between Israel and France — historically one of its close allies and home to more Jews than any other country in Europe — has also become strained in light of the war in Gaza. Advertisement Advertisement Macron last year said Europe must “harden” its collective position on Israel given the dire humanitarian situation in the coastal enclave, and he found some success in convincing other Western democracies to join France in recognizing a Palestinian state last year . Barrot said last week that the recent effort to sanction EU-wide trade with illegal West Bank settlements has been met resistance in Brussels. Jean-Noël Barrot leaves the Elysée Palace in Paris after a meeting on Aug. 31, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images Although several EU countries have pledged to ban trade with the settlements, the move is legally murky under EU law, because trade is an exclusive EU competence. Member countries can do it on the grounds of either national security or violation of human rights and democracy, but any measures at national level are assessed for compatibility with EU law. UNGA looming It comes just two weeks before world leaders meet in New York for the U.N. General Assembly — and ahead of Burnham’s expected first in-person meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump since becoming British prime minister. Miliband said the U.K. will use the gathering to “shine the clearest and harshest spotlight on what is happening and what must change.” In advance of the sanctions statement Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee suggested the U.S. could retaliate against the U.K. over the move. Advertisement Advertisement Huckabee, who over the weekend condemned the government’s “Jew hate” despite Miliband being Jewish, told the BBC that the decision would be a “discrimination against the Jewish people.” He also suggested that individual U.S. states — specifically Florida — might take trade action against the U.K. While Trump has yet to respond to the sanctions, political differences have previously influenced his decisions on trade. In January, the president threatened to impose 10 percent tariffs on eight countries, including the U.K., for opposing his demands to use military force to take control of Greenland. Daria Zakharova, Joshua Berlinger, Camille Gijs, Victor Goury-Laffont and Sue Allan contributed to this report. This developing story has been updated.

https://www.rawstory.com/trump-ai-267793.text: Home Trump U.S. News World Science Video Investigations Ethics Policy About Us 'So pathetic': Finger-wagging Trump aide torched for correcting anchor over new term Bennito L. Kelty September 24, 2026 11:12PM ET Sebastian Gorka, Deputy Assistant to U.S. President Donald Trump, walks to an interview outside the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., December 18, 2025. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo Top White House aide Sebastian Gorka sparked online ire and mockery after he wagged his finger at a Newsmax anchor for using the word "AI." Gorka, the deputy assistant to the president and senior director for counterterrorism at the National Security Council, appeared on Newsmax on Thursday. During an interview , anchor Ed Henry wanted to talk about guardrails for AI when Gorka interrupted him. "No, no, no, no, no, no, no," Gorka said, wagging his finger at Henry. "It's SI. As of this week, it's Super Intelligence." Trump declared during his September 22 UN General Assembly speech that all U.S. documents referring to AI will henceforth call it "super intelligence" because the word "artificial," he argued, "makes intelligence sound fake." The State Department followed through, ordering diplomats in its Bureau of International Organizations to use "super intelligence," The Hill reported . Critics have noted that " super intelligence " already has a specific meaning. Philosopher Nick Bostrom, who popularized the term, defined it as "an intellect that is much smarter than the best human brains in practically every field," and has warned it could pose an existential threat to humanity, Gizmodo noted . Henry didn't push back, telling Gorka, "Thank you for the clarification," but online critics expressed a collective facepalm in response to a clip of the interview. "My God these people are so pathetic," ridiculed columnist and political scientist Richard Hanania. "State-friendly mouthpiece, chastened by a government apparatchik, corrects his wrongspeak," mocked legal analyst and journalist Adam Klasfeld, taking a jab at Newsmax as well. "Most pathetic 'news' interview ever," author and YouTuber Hemant Mehta slammed . "I know we're all inured to bad behavior in the Trump administration," posted Michael A. Cohen, the MS NOW columnist and former government speechwriter. "But Sebastian Gorka is alleged to have been a member of a Hungarian neo-Nazi organization. Today, he works on the National Security Council." (Gorka has denied ties to the Hungarian far-right group.) "Also the name 'Nazi' is hereby changed to 'MAGA,'" blasted TV host and political commentator Keith Olbermann. "It's a cult," chimed in Ron Filipkowski, the editor-in-chief of the MeidasTouch political news network. https://www.theargus.co.uk/news/26583411.text: Court Health Polish doctor paid by East Sussex healthcare ordered to pay out £190k Court Health By Charles Pring Reporter Share 0 Comments (Image: Wikimedia) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A doctor has been ordered to pay more than £190,000 after a High Court judge found he breached his duties as director of a medical services company. Dr Marek Stobinski, a Polish national who has practised in Britain since 2009, was the sole director and shareholder of St Mark Lions Limited, a company used for some of his work as a doctor. Court documents state that Dr Stobinski received payments from East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust between May 2017 and March 2018, which totalled £123,089.30 and went into his personal bank account. The company’s original accounts had wrongly included £123,089 of that personal income as turnover for St Mark Lions Limited. The amended accounts removed it, reducing the company’s recorded turnover for that period from £133,968 to £10,879 and substantially revising its tax position. St Mark Lions entered creditors’ voluntary liquidation in October 2022 after accumulating unpaid corporation tax. Its liquidator, Lloyd Hinton, brought proceedings alleging that Dr Stobinski had breached his responsibilities by failing to distinguish between his interests and those of the company. Following a two-day trial on July 8 and July 9, Deputy ICC Judge Curl KC ordered Dr Stobinski to pay £190,153.99 to the company’s liquidation estate on September 22. The award comprised £112,506 owed through an overdrawn director’s loan account, £39,147.99 in other payments and £38,500 paid directly to him as "management charges". The judge found the company was insolvent or bordering on insolvency by December 2, 2019, when it had £1,218.65 in its bank account and an accumulating tax liability. Its ability to pay creditors depended largely on recovering money owed by Dr Stobinski, but he continued drawing on the company’s funds. A statement of affairs signed in October 2022 placed the corporation tax debt at £79,000. The case also exposed an "almost complete absence" of company books and records. The liquidator received financial statements and some bank statements, but no underlying accounting records, board minutes, dividend resolutions, purchase orders, supplier invoices, asset register or stock list. The court examined more than £63,000 in payments involving Amazon, eBay, PayPal, auctioneers, subscriptions, other companies, pubs and restaurants. Dr Stobinski maintained that the transactions were legitimate business expenditure or were offset by money owed to him. However, the judge found no invoices, purchase orders or other evidence establishing a company purpose and concluded that none of the payments was made for its benefit. The court awarded £39,147.99 under this part of the claim after making an adjustment to avoid possible double-counting. Nine further payments totalling £38,500 were made directly to Dr Stobinski between May 2020 and January 2021 and marked "MGMT CHARGE". Different explanations were offered for the money, including that it represented salary, remuneration or dividends. The judge found the payments should not have been made while the company was financially distressed and dependent on recovering money from its director. Read more Community steps in to protect historic pier amid fears for its future The ten most expensive residential properties sold in Sussex this year 'Incredible sight' - Huge bluefin tuna spotted swimming off the Sussex coast During the trial, Dr Stobinski repeatedly said questions concerning the company should be directed to his accountants. The judge said directors could rely on professional advice but remained "ultimately and inescapably responsible" for their duties. He said: "What has happened in this case is a consequence of Dr Stobinski’s ignorance of what a limited company is and what a director is supposed to do." However, the judge did not accept an allegation that Dr Stobinski had been deliberately dishonest. Court Health Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: India police officers take security measures against a march organised by the main opposition Congress party. Photograph: Yousuf Sarfaraz/Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen India police officers take security measures against a march organised by the main opposition Congress party. Photograph: Yousuf Sarfaraz/Anadolu/Getty Images India Delhi police shut metro stations ahead of election protest march India’s opposition parties and supporters of the ‘cockroach’ youth movement have been demonstrating against a ⁠controversial revision of election voter ⁠lists Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi Mon 12 Oct 2026 01.51 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 09.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Authorities in India’s capital closed six metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions on Monday, as opposition parties planned to march to the supreme court in protest against a ⁠controversial revision of voter ⁠lists that has sparked days ​of unrest in Delhi. Opposition parties and supporters of the “cockroach” youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand the resignation of chief election commissioner ⁠Gyanesh Kumar over the revision that critics say benefits prime minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). The revision that started last year saw over 130 million names – more than the population of Japan – deleted from voter lists during a verification exercise, including 30 million who could not be traced. Others included 28 million people who had died, and 63 million who had relocated. India’s supreme court demands answers over changes to voter roll Read more Opposition parties allege Muslim voters and other minorities, who are unlikely to support the Hindu nationalist ruling party, are disproportionately affected by the deletions – charges both the poll panel and BJP reject. Police detained thousands of protesters in Delhi over the weekend, including leaders ​of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), as supporters of the youth movement ‌sought to march in protest and were ‌stopped by thousands of security personnel who locked down central Delhi. The Election Commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted ‌voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine the country’s democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes. View image in fullscreen Security personnel detain demonstrators during a protest demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner on Sunday. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images Police said the six metro stations were closed on Monday for “security reasons” and traffic restrictions and diversions would be imposed in 20 locations. The main opposition Congress party has announced a march to the supreme court to submit a memorandum to the Chief Justice demanding an end to what it calls “vote theft” and Kumar’s resignation. “Youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the ‌Constitution of India, will walk with us,” Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on X. Chief Justice Surya Kant, however, declined a meeting request in an email, saying Gandhi and the ​Congress delegation should instead approach the court legally since the issue was already being heard by the court and should be addressed through judicial proceedings, a Congress source said. Separately, the CJP said its leaders would meet Delhi police to “demand” a date for a peaceful protest. It has threatened to announce a new call to protest if a date is not given within 24 hours. The youth movement, which has mobilised protests in recent months ⁠against issues ranging from government school infrastructure to jobs, is one of the biggest political challenges to ​Modi and his BJP in his 12 ​years in power. The protests erupted after the ​Indian Express newspaper reported last month that Kumar’s two deputies raised several concerns internally about voter list revisions, ​registration procedures and digital systems. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Police preparing to charge against pupils and students in Paris, France, on 13 October 2026. Photograph: Tonny Linke/NurPhoto/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Police preparing to charge against pupils and students in Paris, France, on 13 October 2026. Photograph: Tonny Linke/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Opinion France French schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truth Rokhaya Diallo To protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is not Sat 17 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 04.53 EDT Share A s a secondary school pupil in 1994, I took part in protests against a reform that would have allowed French employers to pay young people below the minimum wage. Our campaign was successful, but if we had had to face the terrifying police response unleashed on student protesters in France over recent weeks, I would have stayed at home. A 14-year-old boy, Eden, suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out after a police teargas grenade struck him in the face. Sixteen-year-old Maël lost the sight in one eye allegedly after being struck by a shot from an LBD, a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Evan, 15, had his hand blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. And in Dunkirk, a police SUV is alleged to have driven repeatedly at groups of secondary school pupils, as an officer could be heard saying: “Come closer, we’ll smash their fucking faces in.” Accounts from children left terrified by brutal treatment in police custody describe traumatic experiences with severe psychological and physical consequences. France, the self-styled home of human rights, is now attracting the kind of international legal scrutiny you would expect if this were an authoritarian regime gone mad. The human rights organisation Ligue des droits de l’Homme has condemned the alarming “brutalisation of young people”, and the threat to their freedom of expression. A UN special rapporteur has called on the French authorities to respect the physical safety of protesters. The UN human rights office says it is following incidents surrounding the protests in France “with concern”. Amnesty International has called for the suspension of rubber-bullet launchers at school protests, condemned the disproportionate use of force and reminded the authorities of their duty to protect children. The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, whose activism increasingly encompasses struggles against oppression and state violence, travelled to France this week to support school pupils. View image in fullscreen A student checks her smartphone in front of the Helene Boucher high school during a protest in Paris, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Teresa Suarez) Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP It is often argued that France is broke, and that crippling debt levels make the student demand for €10bn of investment to improve their learning conditions a non-starter. But even in our difficult fiscal position, public spending is a political choice: to reduce debt you can cut public spending or you can raise revenue. Economists Élise Huillery and Romane Paris have come up with a credible proposal for investing an additional €11.8bn a year in education, funded through tax reform targeting large inheritances, raising €12.7bn in 2026 and increasing taxes only for the wealthiest 1% of heirs. This would make money available to raise teachers’ pay, improve support for pupils, student grants and housing, and expand university places. But the debate about public spending does not invalidate the legitimate grievances of pupils, teachers and parents, which are not new. Nor does it justify a vicious law and order response. Learning conditions in some of the most disadvantaged schools have been deteriorating to shockingly poor levels for a long time. I highlighted school conditions in France in the Guardian three years ago , arguing then that the state education system was among the most unequal in the developed world. The lack of resources assigned to such basic things as teaching vacancies has been glaringly apparent for years, with jobs in some districts sometimes left unfilled for months. More than 20m teaching hours were lost in state secondary schools in 2024-25, equivalent to almost one in 10 lessons. More than 15m of those hours were lost because no replacement teachers were provided. Schools in designated priority education areas, which serve disadvantaged communities, have been particularly affected, according to France’s National Audit Office . In Seine-Saint-Denis , the poorest part of mainland France, two-thirds of school doctor posts were vacant in 2023. As early as 2022, the Créteil education authority reported a shortfall of 60 school nurses and 20 social workers, with 90% of the unfilled posts in Seine-Saint-Denis. In 2025, 49 suicides were recorded among staff in the national education system. While these deaths cannot all be attributed to work, it is hard to avoid thinking of the severe deterioration in working conditions across the sector. Then there are the schools that are physically falling apart : water that is unsafe to drink because of bacterial contamination, pupils reporting rats and cockroaches , filthy toilets , and in one case, a septic tank that overflows when it rains. There are power cuts, missing furniture and some classrooms are so poorly insulated that temperatures fall below 14C in winter and hit 40C during heatwaves. In Mayotte, where protests began, a secondary school built for 900 pupils is accommodating 2,300. The protests then spread to mainland France through a school in Créteil that began the academic year short of 13 teachers and other staff, as well as a deputy headteacher. Another issue at the core of pupils’ anger is Parcoursup, the system through which school leavers apply for higher education. Seen as discriminatory, it has left 126,000 applicants – many from disadvantaged backgrounds – without a place this year. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Rather than deal with this crisis as justified social protest based on legitimate demands, the government has invoked a doctrine set out in its Operational Guide to Urban Violence. It has treated school pupils as internal enemies to be neutralised. This sets up a coercive response, disregarding the possibility of resolving the conflict through constructive measures. By 8 October, 6,877 people had been taken into police custody, about 80% of them children. On 1 October alone, police made 1,949 arrests, exceeding the highest single-day total recorded since 1961, says the historian Éric Anceau. According to the Syndicat de la magistrature, a French judges’ leftwing union, the numbers reflect a clear determination to crush the movement. So overwhelming has the police deployment been that teachers and parents have had to form human chains to protect children. The police operations are also driven by a focus on arrests, which encourages forceful confrontations and fuels the escalation. This in turn draws more people into rioting. About 700 police officers and a number of teachers have been injured since the start of the unrest. The sociologist Olivier Fillieule points out that policing protests requires an assessment of risk. If the swift break-up a blockade exposes teenagers to serious injury, you have to consider alternatives. Temporarily accepting a degree of disorder when immediate intervention risks creating more of it should remain a guiding principle of policing protests, Filleule says, noting that the French authorities know how to apply restraint when farmers stage blockades. Yet while the police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence, the interior minister Laurent Nuñez said he had given the forces “no instructions to exercise restraint”. This is a shameful and contemptuous way to respond to young people’s healthy expression of dissent. Such violence towards citizens has no place in a democracy. Rokhaya Diallo is a French journalist, film-maker, activist and Guardian Europe columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
